transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lena (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood SE), Rajiv (CTO), Maya (Head of ML), Olivia (Platform), Aaron (Security)

Summary: short discovery to understand Ember's expected steady-state and burst profile, isolation needs (node vs tenant), and security/compliance constraints for a potential Dedicated + Private deployment mix.

Topics: reserved GPUs, isolation strategy, hot-pool prewarm, burst-to-hosted fallback, VPC/on-prem tradeoffs, KMS/keys, SOC2 logs, SLOs and pricing expectations.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, i'm Samir from Redwood. quick intros?
[00:08] Rajiv: yeah, rajiv, cto at ember architects. we're the platform behind their design-automation workflows.
[00:14] Maya: maya, head of ml. i'm responsible for production models and infra ops.
[00:18] Olivia: olivia, platform eng, i'll own the onboarding side.
[00:21] Aaron: aaron, security. i'll be the point on audits and keys.
[00:24] Samir: great. lena and diego from our infra team will go into technical details. first high level: are you leaning more hosted or dedicated today?
[00:34] Rajiv: we're leaning dedicated for latency predictability and data isolation. some workloads can go hosted for bursts but primary traffic needs to be isolated.
[00:42] Lena: thanks. can you give us a sense of steady-state qps or tokens per minute and what your burst multiplier looks like?
[00:50] Maya: steady is about 6 to 8 rps across our text-gen endpoints, peaks up to 5x during product launches, occasionally an 8x for short windows. bursts can last 3-12 minutes.
[01:05] Diego: 8x is pretty aggressive. are those 3-12 minute bursts predictable or ad-hoc?
[01:10] Maya: mostly predictable (release time windows) but sometimes ad-hoc if a partner campaign spikes.
[01:16] Samir: sounds like a reserved pool with reserved capacity for steady-state plus a prewarmed hot-pool for burst handling makes sense. we typically recommend sizing steady pool to cover 1.2x steady for headroom, then a burst band you can either prewarm or fallback to hosted.
[01:32] Rajiv: fallback to hosted worries us from a data-control perspective. we can't send PII off-prem or outside our VPC.
[01:40] Samir: understood. we have private deployment options (VPC endpoint + private control plane) and on-prem combos. for bursts that require strict data residency we can either increase reserved burst capacity or enable cross-region private peering if you have capacity in another region.
[01:56] Aaron: question on KMS: we need HSM-backed keys and rotation policies. do you support customer-managed KMS?
[02:03] Lena: yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and can support BYOK (bring your own key) with rotation. audit logs are captured and we can push to your SIEM.
[02:12] Aaron: good. also SOC2 and ISO?
[02:15] Samir: we're SOC 2 Type II and have ISO in flight, happy to share the package. we'll drop the security pack link.
[02:21] Maya: latency targets — we need p95 < 120ms for short prompts and p99 < 300ms for the multi-turn chat. is that realistic on dedicated?
[02:31] Diego: that depends on model size, sequence length, and batching. for trimmed prompts on 8x A100-equivalent in a dedicated pool we often hit p95 < 100ms for generation up to 256 tokens with KV cache and prefix caching. p99 gets trickier; caching and prefilling helps.
[02:48] Maya: model sizes we're using mostly 13b to 34b distilled variants. we plan to quantize to int8 for cost savings.
[02:55] Lena: int8 quantization is supported; profiling helps to pick the right kernel. we recommend a test run to verify quality vs latency trade-off.
[03:03] Rajiv: on isolation — are we talking node-level isolation or tenant-level? we can't have other customers on the same GPU.
[03:09] Samir: Dedicated pools can be single-tenant (no co-tenancy) and we can pin nodes to your tenant. for extra assurance we can provide segregated racks or even on-prem if you require absolute physical separation.
[03:22] Olivia: what's the expected lead time to reserve, say, 20 GPUs in our region?
[03:27] Lena: typical lead time is 2-4 weeks for reserved pools in high-demand regions; for single-tenant racks or on-prem it can be 6-12 weeks depending on procurement and hardware.
[03:37] Rajiv: cost question — we care about unit economics. how do you price burst vs reserved? is there a blended rate?
[03:44] Samir: reserved capacity is a committed monthly rate; burst is metered at on-demand SKU higher rate. we offer blended pricing for long-term commitments and burst volume commitments. we'll send an example pricing matrix.
[03:54] Maya: curious about prewarm — how do you handle hot-pool prewarming? do you maintain warmed KV cache across models?
[03:59] Diego: we have a hot-pool that keeps a set of models preloaded and optionally keeps a warmed KV cache for recent sessions. warm cache persistence is configurable; it costs GPU memory but reduces cold-start token latency significantly.
[04:13] Maya: do you support pinned embeddings or session affinity?
[04:17] Lena: yes, session affinity and sticky routing can route traffic to the same worker to reuse KV cache. for multi-tenant isolation we can scope affinity to your reserved nodes.
[04:25] Olivia: and autoscaling — how fast can you scale from steady to 5x?
[04:30] Diego: scaling speed depends on whether nodes are prewarmed. if the hot-pool has prewarmed instances, scaling is near-instant (within seconds for request routing). if new nodes need to boot and load model weights that can be minutes. so prewarm the hot-pool for quick jumps.
[04:46] Rajiv: so for our 8x worst-case, we probably need a hot-pool covering at least half that or negotiate a burst commitment from Redwood.
[04:55] Samir: exactly, customers either reserve a baseline + hot-pool sized for expected bursts, or reserve baseline and commit to a predictable burst commit that gives a lower on-demand rate.
[05:05] Aaron: audit logs — retention and access? we need 12 months and the ability to export to our log system.
[05:11] Lena: we support customizable retention; exporting logs to your S3/Cloud storage or directly to SIEM is supported.
[05:18] Maya: any limits around concurrent sessions or KV cache size per session?
[05:22] Diego: it's configurable; KV cache memory depends on model and sequence length. we'll profile with your workloads to give concrete numbers.
[05:30] Rajiv: can you run a synthetic benchmark with our typical prompt mix?
[05:34] Samir: yes, that's the next step — lena will run a bench with a sample prompt set. please share a 24-72 hour sample and spike windows.
[05:42] Maya: we've got anonymized logs we can share, will do.
[05:45] Olivia: what's the SLA for Dedicated?
[05:48] Samir: dedicated has an SLA for uptime and latency tiers; we'll include the SLA language in the pack.
[05:54] Rajiv: also curious about canary rollouts and model version pinning — we need to roll back if quality regressions happen.
[05:59] Lena: Redwood supports pinned model versions per route, canary percentages, and automated fallback to an older model or hosted variant on regressions.
[06:08] Maya: question on telemetry — token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency?
[06:12] Diego: available in the console: token costs, per-model/per-route latency heatmaps, tracing. we can increase retention if you want more history.
[06:19] Rajiv: security follow-up: can you sign a custom BAAs and support our procurement clause on encryption in transit and at rest?
[06:26] Samir: legal has handled BAAs before; we'll surface a template and the security team will follow up.
[06:31] Aaron: for private control plane, how much infra do we manage vs Redwood?
[06:35] Lena: with Private you run the control plane in your VPC and manage networking; Redwood operates the serving runtime optionally in a managed mode. we can do fully managed on-prem if needed.
[06:44] Maya: any gotchas with quantized models on the hot-pool? sometimes the int8 kernels are slower on certain sequences.
[06:50] Diego: true — quantization tradeoffs vary by model. profiling is key. also quantized kernels may use different memory paths impacting prewarm behavior. we'll include profiling results in the bench.
[06:59] Rajiv: are there any customer references using a similar pattern (dedicated + hot-pool + private control plane)?
[07:03] Samir: yes, we'll include anonymized references. one customer in finance uses that exact setup for regulated workloads.
[07:11] Olivia: what does the onboarding timeline look like?
[07:14] Samir: onboarding for dedicated baseline usually 3-6 weeks: contract -> infra prep -> provisioning -> benchmark -> cutover. private/on-prem can extend that.
[07:23] Maya: fine — let's plan to share data and get the bench going.
[07:27] Samir: recap — action items: samir sends pricing and security pack; lena runs benchmark and shares runbook; ember shares traffic and prompt samples; schedule technical feasibility for private with aaron.
[07:40] Rajiv: yep, that works. thanks.
[07:43] Samir: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the docs and a tentative timeline.

References and shared artifacts:
- Benchmark template: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/ember-2026.csv
- Security pack (will be shared): /redwood/security/pack-2026.zip
- Pricing draft (to be shared via email)

End of transcript.
